A person of mass 70 kg stands on the ladder at a fraction 0.6 of its length, measured from its foot. The ladder does not slip. Take g = 9.8 m/s². A hinged shutter is propped open beside the ladder. The angle stated for the ladder is its angle at the outset, and once the person stands on the ladder it is not moved again. The ladder is a wooden ladder with a length of 3.5 m.

What is the magnitude of the total force that the ground exerts on the ladder?
scene_clause: A hinged shutter is propped open beside the ladder. The angle stated for the ladder is its angle at the outset, and once the person stands on the ladder it is not moved again.
scene_object_rationale: A shutter propped open beside the ladder does not touch the ladder, the wall surface it leans on or the ground under it, so the forces on the ladder are unchanged.
sentence: The ladder is a wooden ladder with a length of 3.5 m.
target_phrases: total force that the ground exerts
textbook_familiarity_reason: That the wall force on a ladder does not depend on the ladder's length (the length is in every torque) is a known feature of ladder problems but not a named fact.

A block of mass 0.5 kg is attached to a spring of spring constant 200 N/m and slides on a horizontal frictionless track. What is the amplitude of the steady oscillation of the block?

scene_clause: A heavy door stands in the wall beside the track.
scene_object_rationale: A door in the wall beside the track is not connected to the block, the spring or the damper, so the damping of the block is the stated one.

prompt:

An uncharged cardboard flag stands on the bench beside the apparatus.

What is the magnitude of the initial acceleration of the bead?
scene_clause: An uncharged cardboard flag stands on the bench beside the apparatus.
scene_object_rationale: A cardboard flag on the bench is not part of the ball, the cavity or the bead; it carries no charge that reaches the cavity, so the field in the cavity and the bead are those of the problem.

d_rationale: A clip attached to a flag adds mass to the flag; the bead, the ball and the cavity are unchanged, so the bead's mass and its acceleration are those of the problem.

The air in the neck moves as a rigid plug, with an effective length equal to the neck length plus 0.85 times the neck radius at each end, and it compresses the air in the flask adiabatically. The flask is much smaller than the wavelength of the sound it makes. The speed of sound in the air is 343 m/s. A laboratory funnel stands in a clamp beside the flask, clear of the flask and its neck. The walls of the flask are rigid. A separate tuning fork B in another room sounds at 122 Hz, but it is unrelated to this flask.

One positron annihilates with a free electron that is at rest, and the annihilation produces exactly two photons, which travel along the line of motion of the positron, one forward (in the direction in which the positron moves) and one backward. No other particle is produced. Take the rest energy of the electron and of the positron to be mc² = 511 keV. An ion implanter with its own beam tube and power supplies stands beside the vacuum chamber. The laboratory temperature is 21 °C.

What is the energy of the photon that travels forward?
scene_clause: An ion implanter with its own beam tube and power supplies stands beside the vacuum chamber.
scene_object_rationale: The ions of an implanter beside the chamber are accelerated in a separate tube and do not reach the positrons or the electron that they annihilate with, so the positron energy is the stated one.
sentence: The laboratory temperature is 21 °C.
target_phrases: energy of the photon that travels forward

prompt:
Atoms of mass 23 u move in a beam, each with a kinetic energy of 0.0763 eV. They meet laser light of wavelength 589 nm that is directed against their motion. The frequency of the light is swept so that each atom stays in resonance and keeps absorbing photons until it has stopped. Each absorbed photon is re-emitted in a random direction, so the recoil from the emitted photons averages to zero. The motion is along the beam and non-relativistic, and no other force acts on the atoms. Take h = 6.626e-34 J s. A second oven beside the first makes a second beam of molecules that passes through a nozzle of its own into another chamber.

How many photons must one atom absorb to be brought to rest?
scene_clause: A second oven beside the first makes a second beam of molecules that passes through a nozzle of its own into another chamber.
scene_object_rationale: The molecules of a second oven beside the first pass through their own nozzle into another chamber; a faster nozzle there does not change the kinetic energy of the atoms of the beam that meets the laser light.

d_rationale: A nozzle that speeds up the helium jet does not act on the atoms of the beam; they keep the stated kinetic energy.

The beam makes an angle of 30 degrees with the normal to the mirror. The mirror reflects a fraction 0.9 of the incident light specularly and absorbs the rest. The mirror starts at rest and can move only along a frictionless rail that is normal to its surface. Its speed stays far below c, the beam acts for 24 h, the mirror is in vacuum, and no other force acts along the rail. Heating of the mirror is neglected. Take c = 299800 km/s. A projection screen hangs on a wall of the laboratory, lit by lamps that do not shine on the mirror. Light that a second lamp puts into the beam travels along the beam, and its intensity is measured perpendicular to the beam like that of the beam itself. A second lamp adds 880 W/m² to the intensity of the light that reaches the mirror.

What speed does the mirror reach along the rail?
scene_clause: A projection screen hangs on a wall of the laboratory, lit by lamps that do not shine on the mirror. Light that a second lamp puts into the beam travels along the beam, and its intensity is measured perpendicular to the beam like that of the beam itself.
scene_object_rationale: A projection screen on a wall is lit by its own lamp and is not the mirror; light that reaches the screen does not reach the mirror, so the intensity at the mirror is the stated one.
sentence: A second lamp adds 880 W/m² to the intensity of the light that reaches the mirror.

sentence: A separate crystal B in another laboratory reflects at 12.4 deg, but it is unrelated to this crystal.

A resistance box of 12 Ω is joined across the left gap and a straight sample wire of one uniform material, of length 1.5 m and diameter 0.3 mm, across the right gap. A sliding contact on the bridge wire is joined through a galvanometer to the junction of the box and the sample wire. The galvanometer reads zero when the contact is 41.5 cm from the left end of the bridge wire. The strips, the leads and the contact have negligible resistance, and the wires stay at one steady temperature. A steady cell is joined across the ends of the bridge wire. A lamp on the bench is dimmed by a rheostat wired to a small battery. An extra 9.4 Ω of resistance was joined in series with the box for an earlier trial only.

What is the resistivity of the material of the sample wire?

scene_object_rationale: A lamp dimmed by a rheostat on a battery is a circuit of its own; it carries none of the bridge current, so the balance of the bridge and the resistivity found from it keep their stated values.
sentence: An extra 9.4 Ω of resistance was joined in series with the box for an earlier trial only.

A light disc on one end of the rod drives the air in a long glass tube, which holds a fine dust. Standing waves form in the air at the frequency of the rod, and the dust collects in heaps at the nodes. Take the speed of sound in the air of the tube as 343 m/s. A bar of the same metal lies on a rack beside the bench. Before the clamp is fitted, the bar is lengthened by joining on an extra small amount of the same metal and cross-section.

What is the spacing between adjacent dust heaps?

scene_object_rationale: A bar on a rack is a body of its own; lengthening it changes that bar only, so the clamped rod, the tube and the dust heaps keep their stated values.
sentence: Before the clamp is fitted, the bar is lengthened by joining on an extra small amount of the same metal and cross-section.

The nucleus has a charge number of 1 and a mass of 1836.15 electron masses, and the muon has a mass of 206.77 electron masses. Describe the muon and the nucleus as a two-body Bohr atom with the reduced mass of the pair. The only force between them is the electrostatic attraction, and the recoil of the atom is neglected. Take the Bohr radius of the hydrogen atom to be 0.05292 nm, the Coulomb constant times the elementary charge squared to be 1.44 eV nm and hc = 1240 eV nm. A second apparatus with an electron beam and a vacuum line of its own stands beside the capture chamber. In an earlier capture only, an accelerating gap gave another muon a little more kinetic energy before capture.

What is the wavelength of the emitted photon?

sentence: In an earlier capture only, an accelerating gap gave another muon a little more kinetic energy before capture.

The field is weak enough that every level splits in proportion to the field and all splittings are much smaller than the fine-structure splitting, and all six components of the line are observed. The wavelength shifts are small enough for a first-order treatment. One electronvolt is the elementary charge times one volt, taking the exact SI value of the elementary charge for this conversion only. Take e = 1.602e-19 C, ħ = 1.0546e-34 J s, the electron mass 9.109e-31 kg and hc = 1240 eV nm. A small compass lies on the bench outside the gap of the magnet, far from the vapour, and a field applied at the compass does not reach the vapour. A separate lamp B in another laboratory has two lines that are 26.7 pm apart, but it is unrelated to this vapour.

A pion is lost only by decay, which follows the exponential law in the time that a clock carried by the pion would show, and the pions neither interact with anything nor are absorbed along the tube. All pions have the same momentum and move at constant speed. Take the pion rest energy to be 139.57 MeV, its mean lifetime at rest to be 26.03 ns and c = 2.998e+08 m/s. A cooling-water line runs along the outside of the tube. The cooling-water line is extended by a small amount at its downstream end.

sentence: The laboratory temperature is 21 °C.

prompt:
A probe is to be launched from the surface of a planet so that it just escapes to infinity. The body of the planet is a uniform sphere of radius 3390 km and mean density 3.93 g/cm³, it does not rotate and has no atmosphere, and the pull of any other body is ignored. The Earth is likewise a uniform sphere, of radius 6371 km and mean density 5.51 g/cm³, with an escape speed of 11.19 km/s at its surface. A moon circles the planet.

What speed must the probe have at launch to escape from the surface of the planet?
scene_clause: A moon circles the planet.
scene_object_rationale: A small moon that circles the planet is a different body from the planet; a layer of rock that is added to its radius leaves the radius and the density of the planet, and so the escape speed from its surface, as stated.

d_rationale: A layer of rock that covers the moon changes the moon and not the planet; the planet keeps its stated radius and density.
